title: Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Research Report
name: Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF
tagline: XLP is the low-cost, defensive classic: the S&P 500's grocery, household-goods, beverage and tobacco companies, led by Walmart, Costco, Coca-Cola and Procter & Gamble. After years of lagging, it has had a strong 2026, even as investors pulled money out of it.

chapters.title: What XLP is and where it came from
chapters.lede: XLP launched in December 1998 as one of the original Select Sector SPDRs, which split the S&P 500 into sector funds. It holds the S&P 500's consumer staples companies, about 37 of them, with weights capped for diversification. It is one of the cheapest and most heavily traded sector ETFs, which is why big funds use it.

items: State Street launches the Select Sector SPDRs, including XLP, to slice the S&P 500 by sector.
Staples hold up while tech collapses, which establishes their defensive reputation.
Staples fall far less than the market. People keep buying toothpaste.
With rates near zero, investors buy staples for their dividends, and valuations climb.
Private labels and online upstarts squeeze big food and household brands.
Staples outperform as the market falls and brands push through price increases.
Weight-loss drugs, price fatigue and tariff fears weigh on packaged-food volumes, and staples lag the AI-led market.
Walmart is about 9.7%, Costco about 8.9%, Coca-Cola about 7.4% and P&G about 7.1%. Target is up about 67% YTD while Walmart is down about 5%.
XLP goes from +6.6% YTD in September to about +18% by late October as investors move toward defensives.

chapters.title: What's inside
chapters.lede: XLP is about one-third retailers (Walmart, Costco and Target) and two-thirds brands: beverages, household products, food and tobacco. In 2026 those two groups have moved very differently.

items.title: Retailers vs. brands
items.text: Returns inside the sector have varied widely, so stock-level results drive the fund more than a single sector story would suggest.

blocks.html: Why funds hold XLP: at 0.08% and with deep liquidity, it is a cheap way to add or hedge defensive exposure. That is why quant and multi-strategy funds dominate its 13F holders.

chapters.title: Year by year
chapters.lede: Staples rarely win a bull market, but they usually lose less in bad years. 2022 is the classic example.

chapters.title: What drives it: the macro story
chapters.lede: Staples are supposed to be boring. This cycle has instead brought weight-loss drugs, tariffs and a sector valuation near a ten-year low. Tap a card for the current read on each.

items: People taking GLP-1s eat and snack less, which hurts packaged-food and beverage volumes.
TD Cowen called GLP-1 expansion the most obvious headwind to accelerate in 2026. RBC says the drugs are reshaping categories.
Staples face less direct tariff impact than most sectors because they tend to produce where they sell.
Franklin Templeton worries more about second-order effects, where a new round of tariffs rekindles inflation. Some farm-product tariffs were rolled back.
The sector's multiple relative to the market is near its lowest in a decade.
Franklin Templeton sees limited downside from here. RBC notes the sector's premium to the S&P 500 has been eroding for over 20 years.
After years of price increases, shoppers are trading down to private labels.
Volume recovery is the key ask. Barron's called rekindling demand in 2026 'a tall order' for food makers.
Walmart and Costco gained share with value and scale, and Target rebounded sharply in 2026.
Retailers now carry much of the index's return, so XLP is less of a pure brand play than it used to be.
When growth stocks wobble, investors move to staples.
XLP's late-2026 rally came alongside YTD outflows of $1.75B. The price gain came from the holdings rallying, not from new money into the fund.

chapters.title: Why it's on the radar: the 13F view
chapters.lede: XLP made the Insights tab with 7 tracked holders, up from 5 a year earlier, and steady positive returns over every window. Its 13F story is about trading activity more than conviction.

blocks.html: Huge swings, hedge-style: Two Sigma held about $490M in Q3 2025, cut it to about $40M, and was back near $94M by Q2 2026. Millennium went from $18M to $265M and back to $27M. Swings like these are typical of hedge and pair-trade positions, so read the holder count as interest in the sector, not as stock-picking conviction.

chapters.title: Future outlook: opportunities & risks
chapters.lede: Strategists disagree on staples. Some see cheap valuations and a defensive hedge late in the cycle. Others see a structural volume problem from GLP-1s and private labels. Wells Fargo stays unfavorable, while Franklin Templeton is adding exposure.

opp: The sector's relative multiple is near a 10-year low, which Franklin Templeton says leaves limited downside.
If the AI-led market corrects, staples historically lose much less, as in 2022.
Walmart and Costco keep taking share with scale and value.
Local production limits the direct tariff hit.
At 0.08%, XLP is one of the cheapest ways to hold the sector.
Mature cash-generating companies with long dividend records.
risk: Analysts expect the weight-loss-drug effect on food and beverage volumes to persist.
Shoppers resisting brand price increases cap pricing power.
Broad new tariffs could revive inflation and squeeze margins.
RBC: the sector's valuation premium has been eroding for more than 20 years.
Investors pulled $1.75B YTD even as the price rose.
When growth stocks lead, staples usually trail.

items: GLP-1s and private labels keep volumes falling, brands lose pricing power, and the late-2026 rally fades.
Retailers keep winning but brands stagnate. XLP returns roughly its dividend.

glossary: Exchange-traded fund: a basket of securities that trades on an exchange like a single stock.
State Street's family of ETFs that split the S&P 500 into its sectors.
The annual fee as a share of assets. 0.08% costs 80 cents a year per $1,000 invested.
Money added to minus money withdrawn from a fund. Outflows mean investors are selling shares back.
How easily large amounts trade without moving the price. XLP is very liquid.
Limits on single-stock weights to meet diversification rules.
Companies selling necessities such as food, drinks, household goods and tobacco, which people buy in good times and bad.
Companies selling things people can put off buying, like cars and travel. It is the opposite of staples.
A sector whose earnings hold up in downturns, such as staples, utilities or healthcare.
Store brands, like Costco's Kirkland, that compete with name brands on price.
The ability to raise prices without losing many customers.
Sales growth from selling more units, as opposed to charging more or selling pricier products.
Weight-loss and diabetes drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy that reduce appetite.
The Consumer Analyst Group of New York conference, held each February, where staples companies set their targets.
Investors moving money from one sector or style to another, for example from growth stocks to defensives.
A stock bought mainly for steady dividends, so it trades partly like a bond.
A sector's price-to-earnings multiple compared with the overall market's.
When investors pay a lower multiple for the same earnings.
The percentage drop from a peak to a later low.
An indirect impact, like tariffs raising inflation in general rather than a company's own costs.
A position meant to offset risk elsewhere in a portfolio.
Buying one asset and shorting a related one to bet on the gap between them.
A quarterly SEC report in which investment managers with over $100M list their US-listed long equity positions, including ETFs.
Funds like Two Sigma, Citadel and Millennium that run many models or teams. Their ETF positions often swing quarter to quarter.
